claim: PlyC lyses Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy) on contact.
source: PlyC, a bacteriophage-encoded endolysin, lyses Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy) on contact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of PlyC.

claim: PlyC crosses epithelial cell membranes.
source: We show that the PlyC holoenzyme, mediated by its PlyCB subunit, crosses epithelial cell membranes and clears intracellular Spy in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: PlyCB subunit mediates PlyC crossing of epithelial cell membranes.
source: We show that the PlyC holoenzyme, mediated by its PlyCB subunit, crosses epithelial cell membranes and clears intracellular Spy in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: PlyC clears intracellular Spy in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We show that the PlyC holoenzyme, mediated by its PlyCB subunit, crosses epithelial cell membranes and clears intracellular Spy in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PlyCB interacts strongly with phosphatidylserine (PS).
source: Quantitative studies using model membranes establish that PlyCB interacts strongly with phosphatidylserine (PS), whereas its interaction with other lipids is weak, suggesting specificity for PS as its cellular receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data in the manuscript.

claim: PlyCB interaction with other lipids is weak.
source: Quantitative studies using model membranes establish that PlyCB interacts strongly with phosphatidylserine (PS), whereas its interaction with other lipids is weak, suggesting specificity for PS as its cellular receptor.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by SPR data.

claim: PS is the cellular receptor for PlyCB.
source: Quantitative studies using model membranes establish that PlyCB interacts strongly with phosphatidylserine (PS), whereas its interaction with other lipids is weak, suggesting specificity for PS as its cellular receptor.
evidence: This is suggested based on the strong interaction with PS and weak interaction with other lipids.

claim: PlyC penetrates bilayers above a PS threshold concentration.
source: Neutron reflection further substantiates that PlyC penetrates bilayers above a PS threshold concentration.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by neutron reflection data.

claim: Key residues mediate PlyCB–PS interactions.
source: Crystallography and docking studies identify key residues that mediate PlyCB–PS interactions, which are validated by site-directed mutagenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by crystallography, docking studies, and mutagenesis data.

claim: This is the first report that a native endolysin can traverse epithelial membranes.
source: This is the first report that a native endolysin can traverse epithelial membranes, thus substantiating the potential of PlyC as an antimicrobial for Spy in the extracellular and intracellular milieu and as a scaffold for engineering other functionalities.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the abstract.

claim: Streptococcus pyogenes is a leading human pathogen.
source: Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy), a leading human pathogen, colonizes the skin and mucosal surface, and can lead to severe life-threatening conditions including bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Cunningham, 2000), as well as a variety of superficial infections such as impetigo and pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Streptococcus pyogenes colonizes the skin and mucosal surface.
source: Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy), a leading human pathogen, colonizes the skin and mucosal surface, and can lead to severe life-threatening conditions including bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Cunningham, 2000), as well as a variety of superficial infections such as impetigo and pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Streptococcus pyogenes can lead to bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
source: Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy), a leading human pathogen, colonizes the skin and mucosal surface, and can lead to severe life-threatening conditions including bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Cunningham, 2000), as well as a variety of superficial infections such as impetigo and pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Streptococcus pyogenes can cause impetigo and pharyngitis.
source: Streptococcus pyogenes (Spy), a leading human pathogen, colonizes the skin and mucosal surface, and can lead to severe life-threatening conditions including bacteremia, necrotizing fasciitis, and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Cunningham, 2000), as well as a variety of superficial infections such as impetigo and pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Streptococcal pharyngitis is one of the most common childhood illnesses in the United States.
source: Streptococcal pharyngitis, one of the most common childhood illnesses in the United States, accounts for 15 million outpatient physician visits (Hing et al., 2008) and leads to an estimated economic burden of more than half a billion dollar per year (Pfoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Streptococcal pharyngitis accounts for 15 million outpatient physician visits.
source: Streptococcal pharyngitis, one of the most common childhood illnesses in the United States, accounts for 15 million outpatient physician visits (Hing et al., 2008) and leads to an estimated economic burden of more than half a billion dollar per year (Pfoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Streptococcal pharyngitis leads to an estimated economic burden of more than half a billion dollar per year.
source: Streptococcal pharyngitis, one of the most common childhood illnesses in the United States, accounts for 15 million outpatient physician visits (Hing et al., 2008) and leads to an estimated economic burden of more than half a billion dollar per year (Pfoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Spy-associated diseases are correlated with high mortality and represent a worldwide health concern.
source: Globally, Spy-associated diseases are correlated with high mortality and represent a worldwide health concern (Carapetis et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Many pathogens, including Spy, can invade host cells and survive at low levels in an intracellular niche.
source: The ability of many pathogens, such as Spy, to invade host cells, survive at low levels in an intracellular niche, and seed reinfection poses a major challenge in developing effective treatment protocols to address this carrier state (Rohde and Cleary, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Intracellular pathogens are protected from many antimicrobial agents and host immune effectors.
source: Inside host cells, pathogens are protected from many antimicrobial agents and host immune effectors, and these evasion mechanisms directly contribute to long-term persistence (Helaine et al., 2014; Iovino et al., 2014; Pentecost et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Spy can proliferate within host cells.
source: Spy is well known for its ability to proliferate within host cells (Barnett et al., 2013) and escape autophagic degradation (Sakurai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Spy can escape autophagic degradation.
source: Spy is well known for its ability to proliferate within host cells (Barnett et al., 2013) and escape autophagic degradation (Sakurai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Spy can be recovered from clinical specimens of excised human tonsils, even after antibiotic treatment.
source: Notably, Spy can be recovered from clinical specimens of excised human tonsils (Osterlund et al., 1997), even after antibiotic treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: No effective approach has yet been identified that can specifically kill intracellular Spy.
source: No effective approach has yet been identified that can specifically kill intracellular Spy, although successful strategies have been reported to control other intracellular bacteria, for example, by antibiotics that can accumulate within cells (Ahren et al., 2002; Mandell and Coleman, 2000), encapsulating antibiotics into liposomes or nanoparticles for intracellular delivery (Couvreur et al., 1991), or antimicrobial peptides (Di Grazia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Bacteriophage-encoded endolysins act as peptidoglycan hydrolases.
source: Bacteriophage-encoded endolysins that act as peptidoglycan hydrolases represent a novel class of antimicrobials that kill bacteria by lysing the cell wall.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Endolysins kill bacteria by lysing the cell wall.
source: Bacteriophage-encoded endolysins that act as peptidoglycan hydrolases represent a novel class of antimicrobials that kill bacteria by lysing the cell wall.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: Exogenously applied endolysins kill susceptible Gram-positive bacteria rapidly and with high specificity.
source: Exogenously applied, these enzymes kill susceptible Gram-positive bacteria rapidly and with high specificity (Loessner, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Numerous studies demonstrate the therapeutic potential of endolysins in various animal infection models of human disease.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate the therapeutic potential of endolysins in various animal infection models of human disease, and no adverse side effects have yet been reported (Daniel et al., 2010; Pastagia et al., 2013; Schuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: No adverse side effects of endolysins have yet been reported.
source: Numerous studies demonstrate the therapeutic potential of endolysins in various animal infection models of human disease, and no adverse side effects have yet been reported (Daniel et al., 2010; Pastagia et al., 2013; Schuch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Little is known about endolysins' capacity to penetrate mammalian cells.
source: However, despite a wealth of knowledge about their antibacterial potential, little is known about their capacity, either inherent or conferred by molecular engineering, to penetrate mammalian cells where they could target intracellular pathogens.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: PlyC is a 114 kDa multimeric holoenzyme.
source: One such Spy-specific endolysin, PlyC, has been characterized using biochemical and structural techniques and shown to be a 114 kDa multimeric holoenzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: PlyC comprises one PlyCA subunit and eight identical PlyCB subunits.
source: These studies demonstrated that PlyC comprises one PlyCA subunit, harboring two distinct catalytic domains that work synergistically to cleave two different bonds in the peptidoglycan, and eight identical PlyCB subunits that form a symmetrical ring for cell wall recognition (McGowan et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PlyCA harbors two distinct catalytic domains that work synergistically to cleave two different bonds in the peptidoglycan.
source: These studies demonstrated that PlyC comprises one PlyCA subunit, harboring two distinct catalytic domains that work synergistically to cleave two different bonds in the peptidoglycan, and eight identical PlyCB subunits that form a symmetrical ring for cell wall recognition (McGowan et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Eight PlyCB subunits form a symmetrical ring for cell wall recognition.
source: These studies demonstrated that PlyC comprises one PlyCA subunit, harboring two distinct catalytic domains that work synergistically to cleave two different bonds in the peptidoglycan, and eight identical PlyCB subunits that form a symmetrical ring for cell wall recognition (McGowan et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PlyC has bactericidal activity against Spy in biofilms in vitro.
source: PlyC's bactericidal activity against Spy in biofilms was shown in vitro (Shen et al., 2013), as was its therapeutic potential in an in vivo model of upper respiratory Spy colonization (Nelson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: PlyC has therapeutic potential in an in vivo model of upper respiratory Spy colonization.
source: PlyC's bactericidal activity against Spy in biofilms was shown in vitro (Shen et al., 2013), as was its therapeutic potential in an in vivo model of upper respiratory Spy colonization (Nelson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Rates of Spy adherence ranged from 1 to 5% of the inoculum in co-culture experiments with human epithelial cell lines.
source: In experiments with human epithelial cell lines A549 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or Detroit 562 (data not shown), rates of Spy adherence ranged from 1 to 5% of the inoculum and rates of internalization ranged from 1 to 10% of the adherent streptococci, which are consistent with previous Spy/epithelial cell co-culture studies (LaPenta et al., 1994; Ryan et al., 2001) as well as in vivo findings (Kugelberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-culture experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Rates of Spy internalization ranged from 1 to 10% of the adherent streptococci in co-culture experiments.
source: In experiments with human epithelial cell lines A549 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or Detroit 562 (data not shown), rates of Spy adherence ranged from 1 to 5% of the inoculum and rates of internalization ranged from 1 to 10% of the adherent streptococci, which are consistent with previous Spy/epithelial cell co-culture studies (LaPenta et al., 1994; Ryan et al., 2001) as well as in vivo findings (Kugelberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-culture experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Treatment with 50 μg/ml WT PlyC reduced intracellular colonization by 95% within 1 hr.
source: Although we anticipated the enzymes would need to be engineered with cell penetrating peptides or transduction domains in order to acheive intracellular activity, treatment with 50 μg/ml WT PlyC reduced intracellular colonization (colony forming units; CFUs) by 95% (p<0.001) within 1 hr, and lower concentrations displayed a dose response (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1a.

claim: B30 and Ply700 streptococcal phage endolysins failed to significantly decrease the intracellular Spy CFUs.
source: In contrast, the B30 and Ply700 streptococcal phage endolysins failed to significantly decrease the intracellular Spy CFUs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Roughly 90% of intracellular Spy were eliminated when treated with 50 μg/ml PlyC in primary human tonsillar epithelial cells.
source: Roughly 90% of intracellular Spy were eliminated when treated with 50 μg/ml PlyC (Figure 1b), similar to the effect in immortalized A549 epithelial cells, although the lower dose treatments did not demonstrate significant killing.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The native PlyC holoenzyme can be internalized by mammalian cells.
source: Nonetheless, these data indicate that the native PlyC holoenzyme can be internalized by mammalian cells and that the endolysin retains bacteriolytic efficacy against Spy in the intracellular environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PlyC retains bacteriolytic efficacy against Spy in the intracellular environment.
source: Nonetheless, these data indicate that the native PlyC holoenzyme can be internalized by mammalian cells and that the endolysin retains bacteriolytic efficacy against Spy in the intracellular environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Thirty-minute exposures to 100 μg/ml PlyC revealed no membrane damage compared to Triton X-100 treated controls.
source: Thirty-minute exposures to 100 μg/ml PlyC revealed no membrane damage compared to Triton X-100 treated controls (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a finding from the propidium iodide assay shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A trypan blue dye exclusion assay showed no difference between growth media control and 1 hr treatment with 100 μg/ml PlyC.
source: In addition, a trypan blue dye exclusion assay showed no difference between growth media control and 1 hr treatment with 100 μg/ml PlyC (data not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the trypan blue assay.

claim: Exposure to or internalization of PlyC does not compromise the membrane integrity of epithelial cells.
source: Both assays suggest that exposure to or internalization of PlyC does not compromise the membrane integrity of epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the propidium iodide and trypan blue assays.

claim: Fluorescently labeled PlyC and PlyCB, but not PlyCA, are internalized in A549 cells upon incubation.
source: At a concentration of 5 μg/ml, both the fluorescently PlyC holoenzyme and the PlyCB octamer, but not the PlyCA subunit, were internalized by A549 epithelial cells within 30 min (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Internalized PlyC and PlyCB accumulate in vesicle-like structures with diameters of ≈0.5 μm.
source: Both internalized PlyC and PlyCB were found to accumulate in vesicle-like structures with diameters of ≈0.5 μm.
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: WT PlyC colocalizes with intracellular Spy.
source: Wild type (WT) PlyC, with full bacteriolytic activity, colocalized with intracellular Spy (Figure 2c, merged image in the lower middle panel), where ruptured Spy cell walls are visible.
evidence: This is a finding from the confocal microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2c.

claim: PlyCB mediates translocation of the PlyC holoenzyme across the plasma membrane.
source: Taken together, the data show that the subunit PlyCB mediates translocation of the PlyC holoenzyme across the plasma membrane, where it is subsequently trafficked and quantitatively lyses intracellular Spy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PlyC quantitatively lyses intracellular Spy.
source: Taken together, the data show that the subunit PlyCB mediates translocation of the PlyC holoenzyme across the plasma membrane, where it is subsequently trafficked and quantitatively lyses intracellular Spy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: At neutral pH, the PlyCB octamer is net positive (pI = 8.5).
source: At neutral pH, the PlyCB octamer is net positive (pI = 8.5), and its solvent accessible surface contains 48 cationic residues, two arginines and four lysines on each monomer (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: The solvent accessible surface of PlyCB octamer contains 48 cationic residues, two arginines and four lysines on each monomer.
source: At neutral pH, the PlyCB octamer is net positive (pI = 8.5), and its solvent accessible surface contains 48 cationic residues, two arginines and four lysines on each monomer (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: PlyC(PlyCBK70E,K71E) and PlyC(PlyCBK23E) were fully active in external Spy degradation.
source: The holoenzymes incorporating PlyCBK23E and PlyCBK70E,K71E were fully active in external Spy degradation, but PlyC(PlyCBK59E) and PlyC(PlyCBR66E) only had ≈15% and 1% of WT PlyC activity, respectively (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the turbidity reduction assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PlyC(PlyCBK59E) had ≈15% of WT PlyC activity.
source: The holoenzymes incorporating PlyCBK23E and PlyCBK70E,K71E were fully active in external Spy degradation, but PlyC(PlyCBK59E) and PlyC(PlyCBR66E) only had ≈15% and 1% of WT PlyC activity, respectively (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the turbidity reduction assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PlyC(PlyCBR66E) had 1% of WT PlyC activity.
source: The holoenzymes incorporating PlyCBK23E and PlyCBK70E,K71E were fully active in external Spy degradation, but PlyC(PlyCBK59E) and PlyC(PlyCBR66E) only had ≈15% and 1% of WT PlyC activity, respectively (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the turbidity reduction assay shown in Figure 3b.

claim: PlyCBR66E mutant lacks binding to Spy.
source: Fluorescence microscopy showed a lack of binding of the PlyCBR66E mutant to Spy while PlyCBK23E and PlyCBK59E, as well as a charge-conserving PlyCBR66K mutant bound comparably to WT (Figure 3c, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PlyCBK23E, PlyCBK59E, and charge-conserving PlyCBR66K mutant bind to Spy comparably to WT.
source: Fluorescence microscopy showed a lack of binding of the PlyCBR66E mutant to Spy while PlyCBK23E and PlyCBK59E, as well as a charge-conserving PlyCBR66K mutant bound comparably to WT (Figure 3c, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PlyCBK23E, PlyCBK59E, and PlyCBR66E mutants lost the ability to enter A549 epithelial cells.
source: Moreover, the PlyCBK23E, PlyCBK59E, and PlyCBR66E mutants, but not PlyCBR66K, lost the ability to enter A549 epithelial cells (Figure 3c, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: PlyCBR66K mutant retains the ability to enter A549 epithelial cells.
source: Moreover, the PlyCBK23E, PlyCBK59E, and PlyCBR66E mutants, but not PlyCBR66K, lost the ability to enter A549 epithelial cells (Figure 3c, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the fluorescence microscopy experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: K23 of PlyCB is not involved in Spy binding but is involved in epithelial cell internalization.
source: Thus, K23 of PlyCB is not involved in Spy binding but is involved in epithelial cell internalization, whereas K59 and, to a greater extent, R66 are involved in both Spy binding and internalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and microscopy experiments.

claim: K59 and R66 of PlyCB are involved in both Spy binding and internalization.
source: Thus, K23 of PlyCB is not involved in Spy binding but is involved in epithelial cell internalization, whereas K59 and, to a greater extent, R66 are involved in both Spy binding and internalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and microscopy experiments.

claim: Electrostatic interaction involving R66 plays a significant role in PlyCB targeting both the Spy cell wall and the epithelial surface.
source: In addition, the response of the charge-conserving PlyCBR66K mutant supports the hypothesis that electrostatic interaction involving R66 plays a significant role in PlyCB targeting both the Spy cell wall and the epithelial surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: An excess of heparin or CS-B did not block PlyCB internalization into A549 epithelial cells.
source: An excess of heparin or CS-B did not block PlyCB internalization into A549 epithelial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is a finding from the competition experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of A549 cells with chondroitinase ABC or heparinase III prior to PlyCB incubation did not abrogate PlyCB internalization.
source: Furthermore, treatment of A549 cells with chondroitinase ABC or heparinase III prior to PlyCB incubation did not abrogate PlyCB internalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), ruling out a role for these GAGs as a PlyCB receptor.
evidence: This is a finding from the enzyme treatment experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GAGs do not play a role as a PlyCB receptor.
source: Furthermore, treatment of A549 cells with chondroitinase ABC or heparinase III prior to PlyCB incubation did not abrogate PlyCB internalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e), ruling out a role for these GAGs as a PlyCB receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enzyme treatment experiments.

claim: WT PlyCB interacts with phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidic acid (PA), and phosphatidylserine (PS) but not with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylcholine (PC), or any of the phosphatidylinositides.
source: A phosphoinositide array (PIP Strip) showed that WT PlyCB interacts with phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidic acid (PA), and phosphatidylserine (PS) but not with phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylcholine (PC), or any of the phosphatidylinositides (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the binding has elements of specificity.
evidence: This is a finding from the phosphoinositide array shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: PlyCBK59E and PlyCBR66E lost the ability to bind PI and showed diminished binding to PA and PS.
source: PlyCBK59E and PlyCBR66E that lack the ability to internalize in epithelial cells also lost the ability to bind PI and showed diminished binding to PA and PS.
evidence: This is a finding from the phosphoinositide array experiments.

claim: PlyCB binds phospholipids with largely different affinities.
source: Typical SPR traces (Figure 4a,b) show that PlyCB binds phospholipids with largely different affinities and is presumably differentially organized at the surface of DOPC membranes that contain below and above 15 mol% 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (DOPS).
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: At 10 mol% PS, adsorbed PlyCB washes out in a buffer rinse.
source: At 10 mol% PS, adsorbed PlyCB washes out in a buffer rinse whereas it is largely retained upon rinsing in membranes with 20 mol% PS.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: At 20 mol% PS, adsorbed PlyCB is largely retained upon rinsing.
source: At 10 mol% PS, adsorbed PlyCB washes out in a buffer rinse whereas it is largely retained upon rinsing in membranes with 20 mol% PS.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Changes in electrical membrane characteristics were minimal upon PlyCB binding at 30 mol% PS.
source: The Cole-Cole plot in Figure 4c, obtained with 30 mol% PS at the highest PlyCB concentration, illustrates that changes in electrical membrane characteristics were minimal.
evidence: This is a finding from the EIS experiments shown in Figure 4c and Table 1.

claim: PlyCB binds poorly to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and PI.
source: PlyCB binds poorly to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and PI and shows only low affinity to PA.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: PlyCB shows only low affinity to PA.
source: PlyCB binds poorly to phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and PI and shows only low affinity to PA.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: PlyCB binding to 30 mol% PS is extremely strong.
source: In contrast, PlyCB binding to 30 mol% PS is extremely strong.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: At PS ≥20 mol%, the adsorption isotherms followed Hill functions with N > 1.
source: At PS ≥20 mol%, the adsorption isotherms no longer followed a Hill function with N = 1 (i.e., a simple Langmuir isotherm) but were well described by Hill functions with N > 1 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR data analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: On membranes that contained 30 mol% PS, the affinity of PlyCB is Kd = 40 ± 10 nM.
source: On membranes that contained 30 mol% PS, both the affinity of the protein (Kd = 40 ± 10 nM) and its surface density were very high.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR data analysis.

claim: At 15 mol% PS, the Kd of PlyCB increases to ≈0.5 μM.
source: At 15 mol% PS, the Kd increases to ≈0.5 μM, and at 10 mol% PS, PlyCB binding is reduced to the level of binding equal to 30 mol% PI or PG.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR data analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There is a threshold of PlyCB binding to PS-containing bilayers, where membranes at PS concentrations >15 mol% behave differently from membranes at ≤15 mol%.
source: This suggests that there is a threshold of PlyCB binding to PS-containing bilayers, where membranes at PS concentrations >15 mol% behave differently from membranes at ≤15 mol%.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SPR data analysis.

claim: The affinity of PlyCB to PC:PA:PS = 70:20:10 membrane was higher (Kd ≈ 1.2 μM) than to membranes with 10 mol% of PS or 30 mol% PA as the only anionic lipid.
source: We measured the affinity of the protein to an stBLM composed of PC:PA:PS = 70:20:10 (Figure 5c) and observed that the affinity was higher (Kd ≈ 1.2 μM) than to membranes with 10 mol% of PS or 30 mol% PA as the only anionic lipid, but not as strong as to stBLMs containing ≥20 mol% PS.
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 5c.

claim: PlyCBR66E binds poorly to PS, comparable with WT PlyCB to PI-containing membranes.
source: As expected, this mutant binds poorly to PS, comparable with WT PlyCB to PI-containing membranes (compare Figure 5d and Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the SPR experiments shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Both electrostatic attraction and specific binding contribute to PlyCB interacting with the membrane.
source: The observed threshold in PlyCB binding to PS-containing membranes suggests that both electrostatic attraction and specific binding contribute to PlyCB interacting with the membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SPR data analysis.

claim: At 15 mol% PS, PlyCB forms a diffuse layer of protein that extends about 200 Å out from the bilayer surface.
source: At 15 mol% PS, PlyCB forms a diffuse layer of protein that extends about 200 Å out from the bilayer surface (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7a.

claim: At 15 mol% PS, protein insertion into the membrane is negligible.
source: Moreover, protein insertion into the membrane is negligible.
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7a.

claim: At 30 mol% DOPS, PlyCB is deeply inserted in the membrane and spans its entire thickness, headgroup to headgroup.
source: Figure 7b shows the CVO profile of the protein on DOPC:DOPS 70:30 at cp = 600 nM. The protein is deeply inserted in the membrane and spans its entire thickness, headgroup to headgroup.
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Some protein is superficially adsorbed at a distance of ≈20 Å above the membrane surface at 30 mol% DOPS.
source: Some protein is superficially adsorbed as evidenced by a protein CVO peak at a distance of ≈20 Å above the membrane surface.
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Flushing the membrane with protein-free buffer removed superficially adsorbed protein.
source: Flushing the membrane with protein-free buffer removed this adsorbed protein, as shown in Figure 7c.
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7c.

claim: PlyCB protein retained within the membrane is almost symmetrically distributed across the tethered bilayer and occupies up to 10% of its volume.
source: The CVO profile after the flush shows that the PlyCB protein retained within the membrane is almost symmetrically distributed across the tethered bilayer and occupies up to 10% of its volume.
evidence: This is a finding from the neutron reflection experiments shown in Figure 7c.

claim: The inserted protein spans the bilayer at a well-defined angle that leads to a match with the bilayer thickness.
source: This rigid body modeling approach (Figure 7c, black trace) resembled the protein distribution determined in a spline fit (Figure 7c, red trace), which suggests that the inserted protein spans the bilayer at a well-defined angle that leads to a match with the bilayer thickness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neutron reflection data analysis.

claim: The crystal structures of PlyC holoenzyme and PlyCB octamer reveal a shallow, charged groove on the PlyCB membrane-binding surface surrounded by residues R29, K59, and R66.
source: The crystal structures of both the PlyC holoenzyme and the PlyCB octamer (PDB: 4F88 and 4F87, respectively; Figure 3a) reveal a shallow, charged groove on the PlyCB membrane-binding surface surrounded by residues R29, K59, and R66 (Figure 3a, inset).
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: The groove is a binding site for anionic lipids.
source: In combination with the residues identified to affect intracellular translocation, this suggests that the groove is a binding site for anionic lipids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the crystal structure and mutagenesis data.

claim: A 1.7-Å X-ray crystal structure of PlyCBR66E was determined.

claim: Extracellular Spy remains uniformly sensitive to penicillin.
source: While extracellular Spy remains uniformly sensitive to penicillin, treatment failures are common because Spy can invade human host cells and adopt an intracellular niche (LaPenta et al., 1994; Marouni and Sela, 2004; Nobbs et al., 2009) where the antibiotic is unable to penetrate.

claim: Internalization is implicated in recurring streptococcal infection.
source: Internalization is implicated in recurring streptococcal infection because Spy can escape from endosomes and enter the cytosol in a streptolysin O-dependent manner, induce apoptosis of host cells, and subsequently repopulate the mucosal surface after antibiotic prophylaxis ends (Ogawa et al., 2011; O'Seaghdha and Wessels, 2013; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: There have not been reports of wild type endolysins internalizing a eukaryotic cell.

claim: PlyC internalization is a three-step process that involves membrane binding through electrostatic interaction and specific ligation with PS, cellular entry by caveolae-dependent endocytosis, and cytosolic transport where PlyC comes into contact with intracellular Spy.
source: We propose that PlyC internalization is a three-step process that involves (1) membrane binding through electrostatic interaction and specific ligation with PS, (2) cellular entry by caveolae (or lipid raft)-dependent endocytosis, and (3) cytosolic transport where PlyC comes into contact with intracellular Spy.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: TAT-mediated protein transduction occurs in a similar pathway to PlyC internalization.
source: Interestingly, TAT-mediated protein transduction was reported to occur in a similar pathway (Gump and Dowdy, 2007), suggesting that PlyC internalization is comparable to cellular uptake of TAT.

claim: PlyC has potential as a topical agent to combat refractory streptococcal infection on the skin and mucosal surface.
source: With the large pool of endolysins that bear distinct functional domains, our results not only show the potential of PlyC as a topical agent to combat refractory streptococcal infection on the skin and mucosal surface, but also provide a rationale to further investigate the intracellular potential of endolysins against other intracellular pathogens in a species-specific manner.
